11. Do a spellcheck pass

Or ask a friend to do it! If one of the first textboxes in your game has a typo, that's really, really offputting. Sorry!

Also, a lot of text-heavy demos I've played this year have NOT used enough commas. That might be a personal thing, but it really bothers me!

10. Consider how your game launches

People are playing your demo on Steam Deck and Macbook, as well as PC. Make sure you've got different aspect ratios as options, because I played quite a few demos that had a bunch of useful UI cropped off the top and bottom of my screen :/

9. Don't default to the first 20 minutes

The intro to your game is probably really cool BUT that does not always make it a good demo. The start of a game can be slow, long, and 90% tutorial, when what a player might want is something more representative of the game as a whole.

8. Please god let me skip text

Please please PLEASE don't have slow-typed-out-walls-of-text that play every time I launch the game, or I will claw out my own eyeballs. You would not believe how many demos I've played that do this. Thank you

7. Don't be afraid to get weird!

If you've got the time... block off non-demo areas with traffic cones! Add a big beefy bodyguard who won't let you into certain dialogues! Or, you know, something that fits your game's vibes. The demo is a playground, so why not have a little fun with it?

6. Custom demos might be worth it

Consider making something custom if your game might benefit from the effort. This year, The Dungeon Experience did a fantastic job of making a weird, meta demo, tangential to the actual game, and it absolutely made it stand out from the rest.

5. Don't put your demo into Next Fest if it's not ready

This is your chance to make a splash, so it's a bit of a letdown when your demo is very very very unpolished/unfinished. This might be your *only* chance at a first impression for some players. Make the most of it!

4. Get to the point faster

Don't make me sit through a super-long intro cutscene or a long, boring conversation as the very first thing I do. You have, like, 10 minutes to sell your game, so let me get into the meat of the game ASAP, or at least give me some actions/choices to hook me in!

3. You don't need that much text

An excellent general tip for tutorials, Steam store page copy, dialogue, item descriptions, and more!

Choose your words deliberately and you'll be able to communicate more effectively, and you won't lose people's attention as fast.

2. If you're gonna copy [GAME], at least make an effort

There are sooo many low-effort ripoffs of Balatro this year. It makes sense, but like... try harder to be unique! Your game could have really great mechanics, but if it looks EXACTLY like Balatro, I'm gonna think less of it automatically.

1. Your game is too loud

I have had to turn down the volume from 100% to 20% on EVERY. SINGLE. DEMO this year.  Launch your game at 30-50% volume, and let me turn it up if I need to! It hurts my delicate ears! :<
